summary: Delhi sits on the dead-flat floor of California's San Joaquin Valley, a 3.5-square-mile census-designated community just south of Turlock where the horizon line is defined not by hills but by almond orchards, dairy operations, and irrigation canals — and where a median home price of roughly $339,000 against a median household income of about $66,300 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5.1, making homeownership strained but not impossible in a state where ratios of 8 or 10 are common in coastal metros. The economy here is firmly agricultural and food-processing; major employers in the surrounding area include large dairy and poultry operations, and Turlock's distribution and packaging facilities are a short drive north on Highway 99, which bisects the region and doubles as the default commute corridor. With average daily highs around 78°F and 9.5 hours of sunshine, summers are genuinely hot and winters mild but foggy — the tule fog that blankets the Central Valley from November through February is a defining, sometimes hazardous, feature of daily life. Rent at a median of $1,262 is remarkably low by California standards, though the poverty rate of 16.5% signals that even those rents press hard on a meaningful share of households. Delhi is a place where the cost of living is shaped almost entirely by agriculture's rhythms, and the tradeoff is distance — roughly 90 miles to the Bay Area, 60 to Yosemite — which keeps prices accessible and options limited in roughly equal measure.
